name: Crocin (saffron constituent)
short: Type 2 diabetes meta-analysis: creatinine rose after crocin (before-after; comparator not stated). 1-month trial, 44 healthy adults: no major adverse events; lower amylase, mixed white cells, PTT.
text: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials of saffron and crocin in people with type 2 diabetes (14 at moderate risk of bias), which pooled before-and-after mean differences, found HbA1c, fasting blood glucose and systolic blood pressure lower but creatinine levels higher after crocin (the abstract does not say whether these changes were compared with a control group, how many of the trials tested crocin, or the units of the creatinine change); the authors judged saffron extract to be superior because it was effective on more measures and did not induce adverse effects. In a one-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 44 healthy volunteers taking crocin tablets, no major adverse events were reported, and blood, biochemical, hormonal and urine measures did not change except for decreases in amylase, mixed white blood cells and PTT (a blood-clotting time); the authors described a relatively safe profile within the trial period. In an 8-week randomised trial in people with Parkinson's disease, crocin was reported as well tolerated with minimal side effects; the abstract does not list them. A 2014 review states that crocin showed no major toxicity in experimental models; the abstract does not say what those models were. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
